opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way we think about it is that the hard part of a humanoid isn't the application. It's the foundation underneath it. If you get the core platform right, meaning the body, the actuators, the perception stack, and the software that lets the robot understand and move through human environments, then the difference between a warehouse job and a defense job is mostly at the edges.

So we start from a simple premise: the world is built for people. Stairs, doorways, door handles, vehicles, tools, shelving. A factory floor and a forward operating base have a lot more in common than people assume. Both are messy, unstructured, built around the human form, and full of dull, dirty, or dangerous work. A robot that can carry a load, open a door, climb a step, and use a tool designed for a human hand is useful in both places.

In practice, we keep one common hardware platform and one common autonomy core, and then we specialize through software, payloads, and the operating envelope. On the commercial side, that might mean logistics, material handling, or inspection, with an emphasis on uptime, cost per hour, and working safely next to people. On the defense side, the same robot might do logistics resupply, explosive hazard work, or reconnaissance in places you don't want to send a soldier first. The requirements shift. You care more about ruggedization, operating with degraded or no connectivity, security of the communications and the software supply chain, and very clear human control over what the robot does.

That last point matters a lot to us. Across both markets we design around a human-in-the-loop model. The robot handles the physical risk and the repetitive work, and a person stays responsible for the judgment calls. That's good engineering, and it's also how you earn trust with customers, whether that's an operations manager or a commander.

There's also a real benefit to serving both markets. Defense pushes you on reliability and toughness in a way commercial customers often don't, and commercial scale drives down cost and speeds up iteration in a way defense alone never could. Each side makes the product better for the other. The discipline is not letting the platform fork into two separate products. Once you do that, you lose the economies of scale that make humanoids viable in the first place.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that we don't think of it as two products, or even two markets. We think of it as one platform and a set of missions, and the platform has to be boring in the best possible way: reliable, hardened, and predictable, whether it's unloading a truck or walking a perimeter.

What most people get wrong is assuming the defense side wants something exotic. It doesn't. The military has the same core problems a warehouse has, just with worse conditions and higher stakes. They want something that can lift, carry, open doors, climb stairs, and keep working in heat, cold, dust, and rain, with no engineer standing behind it. If you build for that environment first, the commercial version is almost a relaxation of the spec. If you build for a clean, climate-controlled factory floor first and then try to ruggedize it, you end up redesigning the whole thing.

So the hardware is common. Where the two worlds diverge is in the software stack and the policy layer around it. On the commercial side the behaviors are about throughput and safety around people who aren't paying attention to the robot. On the defense side it's about operating with degraded communications, carrying heavy loads over bad terrain, and keeping a human in the loop for anything that matters. We've been very deliberate that the robot is a logistics and labor asset. It carries, it moves, it inspects. We draw a clear line there and we say that out loud, because it matters to our customers on both sides.

The other thing that makes it work is volume. Defense alone would never give you the unit economics to build a humanoid that's affordable. Commercial alone doesn't push you hard enough on durability. Doing both means every robot that goes into a distribution center is also running the same locomotion and manipulation stack we'll ship to a base, and every lesson from the field flows back into the same codebase. One product, one supply chain, one team learning from every deployment. That's the whole strategy.

astra-6.text:
I think you start with what those environments have in common. The robot has to move through spaces designed for people, handle objects, and do useful work reliably. You want that core platform to stay consistent, rather than building a completely different robot for every customer.

Then you adapt it to the task. Moving supplies in a commercial facility and moving supplies in a defense setting may share a lot of capabilities, but the operating conditions, communications, and safety requirements can be very different. Those differences need to shape how you deploy and validate the system.

The key is to be specific about the job. A humanoid form doesn’t automatically make a robot useful. Pick a task, prove that it can do it consistently, and expand from there.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you start with the tasks they have in common. Moving through a building, carrying something, inspecting an area—those capabilities can be useful in both a business and a defense setting. So you build a common platform around mobility, manipulation, and perception, and then adapt it to the job.

The challenge is that the operating requirements can be very different. A predictable indoor environment is one thing; an unfamiliar, demanding environment is another. You have to be clear about what the robot can reliably do, how people supervise it, and what happens when it encounters something it can’t handle. The goal is a shared foundation with the right capabilities and safeguards for each application.
